newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan says new Iraq oil deal adds $70 mln burden.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says new Iraq oil deal adds $70 mln burden.

text.p: Jordan said on Monday that a decision by Iraq to raise its oil pricing terms under a newly renewed "oil-for-trade" barter deal by 27 percent will add an extra $70 million burden to its deficit-ridden budget.

Trade and Industry Minister Ali Abu al-Ragheb said Iraq set a $19 per barrel price tag under its newly concluded 1997 oil supply deal, part of a wider protocol under which sanction-hit Baghdad supplies Amman with around 75,000 bpd of crude oil and petroleum products in exchange for Jordanian goods,

The state news agency Petra quoted Abu al-Ragheb as saying that although Iraq raised prices by $4 per barrel from last year's level, Baghdad was still offering the kingdom "excellent preferrential prices," significantly below world market prices.

Jordanian ministers signed the deal on Saturday in Baghdad under the new terms after Iraq refused to keep last year's preferrential terms in tact. Baghdad insisted that steep oil prices warranted a reduction in the discount offered last year, officials said.
Jordan's higher $19 per barrel price terms for nearly half the energy supplies it imports would add an estimated $70-$75 million to its budget burden, Abu al-Ragheb said.
This was even after factoring in Iraq's agreement to supply Jordan with an extra $50 million dollars worth of free oil in 1997 on top of last year's $250 million portion, the minister said.

Jordanians say that the free portion goes to settle old debts which Iraq has incurred over the years. Iraq also secured a higher trade protocol ceiling by $35 million to $250 million for 1997 in return for raising the free oil component of its oil.
Jordan last year cut by half the value of goods it sent to Iraq to around $220 million, saying Baghdad's debts stood at around $1.2 billion and were increased by each annual protocol.
Jordan's oil purchases from Iraq are exempt from United Nations sanctions on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Jordan has been totally dependent on Iraq for its oil supplies since Saudi Arabia stopped the flow of an estimated 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude to punish Amman for its pro-Iraqi sympathies during the 1991 Gulf War that ousted Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
